Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: McKesson is a dominant, well-run incumbent rather than a Rule Breaker: it leads a mature three-player drug distribution industry, has strong price momentum (about +24% over 12 months) and good management, but lacks a fast-emerging industry, a consumer brand or a visionary founder.
summaries.buffett: McKesson has a durable scale-based position, predictable demand and heavy buybacks (diluted shares down from 160.6M in FY2021 to 124.1M in FY2026), which fit Buffett's taste for understandable businesses. Thin 1.5% operating margins, weak pricing power against concentrated customers, a past opioid liability and a price of about 22.5x forward adjusted EPS limit the margin of safety.
summaries.munger: The business is simple and hard to dislodge in an oligopoly with Cencora and Cardinal, and it compounds per-share earnings through negative working capital and buybacks. Munger would note the opioid history as a lesson in incentives and would see the stock as fairly to fully priced rather than a bargain.
summaries.lynch: McKesson is a classic stalwart turned faster grower, with revenue up 12.4% and adjusted EPS up 18% in FY2026 and a 13-16% long-term EPS growth target. At about 22.5x forward adjusted EPS the PEG is around 1.5, so it is no longer the cheap boring stock Lynch liked, though the story is easy to follow.
summaries.fisher: Management has steadily added higher-value oncology, retina and technology services and executes well, but McKesson does little R&D and its main product is a commodity service. It partly fits Fisher's focus on management quality and growth runway, less so on product innovation and margins.
summaries.graham: McKesson fails most of Graham's defensive tests: it had a net loss in FY2021, trades at about 35x three-year average GAAP EPS, has negative book value and a current ratio of 0.89. It does pass on size and a long dividend record.
summaries.thiel: McKesson does not fit Zero to One well: it has no proprietary technology that is 10x better, and it competes in a mature oligopoly rather than creating a new market. Its strengths are distribution and durability, two of Thiel's seven questions.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's focus on durable growth at a reasonable price and on operating discipline partly fits: revenue grew 12.4% with falling operating expenses and heavy buybacks in FY2026. But this is not a secular-technology compounder, growth is expected to slow to about 7%, and the stock already trades near analysts' average target.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings momentum is good (guidance raised to $44.20-$45.00 adjusted EPS for FY2027 after a Q1 beat) and the stock is at record highs, which suits Druckenmiller's trend-following. The thesis lacks a big macro or liquidity tailwind and a large asymmetric catalyst.
summaries.smith: McKesson converts profit to cash and earns high returns on its small capital base, but Terry Smith prefers high gross margins and pricing power, and McKesson's 3.6% gross margin and customer concentration fall short. At about a 4.6% free-cash-flow yield it is not overpriced, but it is not a typical Fundsmith company.
summaries.greenblatt: Return on capital is very high because working capital is negative, which scores well on the Magic Formula. The earnings yield is middling, with FY2026 operating income about 5.1% of enterprise value.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool partly fits: the business model is solid and management allocates capital well through buybacks and acquisitions in oncology. Reinvestment opportunities at high returns are limited because the core business needs little capital and grows with drug spending.
summaries.pabrai: McKesson is a simple, low-risk business with a small chance of permanent loss, but it is not a distressed or mispriced Dhandho bet. At record highs with about 22.5x forward earnings, there is no 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup.
summaries.wood: McKesson does not fit ARK's disruptive-innovation framework: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing. Its oncology data and technology services are incremental rather than exponential platforms.
summaries.ackman: McKesson fits several of Ackman's criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with high barriers to entry and limited exposure to extraneous factors. Weaker points are the reliance on drug-pricing policy and a valuation that no longer offers a large discount to intrinsic value.
summaries.sleep: McKesson uses scale to buy and deliver drugs more cheaply than smaller rivals, a partial version of Sleep's scale-economies-shared model, but the savings largely go to concentrated customers through price competition rather than building a virtuous cycle of loyalty. Its position should remain strong but not clearly stronger in 20 years.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge new markets and transformative technology; McKesson is a mature distributor in an established market. It solves a real, painful logistics problem but would not fit a Sequoia-style investment.
summaries.nash: McKesson fails many of Nash's instant-kill tests (more debt than cash, operating margin 1.5%, consensus growth about 7%) and scores about 50 of 130 on his 13 categories. At $1,004.84 the Nash-style DCF gives about $814 per share at a 12% discount rate, so it does not pass his valuation steps despite consistent earnings beats.

momentum.evidence: The stock rose from $811.34 at the end of October 2025 to $1,004.84 on October 16, 2026 (+24%), versus about +12% for the S&P 500 (6,840 to 7,659), and hit a record high in October 2026.

g4.evidence: CEO Brian Tyler has a strong execution record and institutions own about 85% of the shares, and Apollo Funds bought about 13% of the Medical-Surgical business for $1.25B in June 2026, but there is no famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: At $1,004.84 the stock trades above the average analyst target of about $983-1,001, with RBC at Hold and $845, but most analysts (13 of 16) still rate it a Buy rather than calling it overvalued.

simple.evidence: McKesson buys medicines from manufacturers and delivers them to pharmacies, hospitals and clinics for a small markup and fees, a business a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue has grown every year from $238.2B in FY2021 to $403.4B in FY2026 and adjusted EPS from $17.21 to $39.11, but GAAP results swung to a $(4,539)M loss in FY2021 because of opioid charges.

integrity.evidence: Management is rational with capital (repurchasing $4,750M of stock in FY2026) and pay is tied to EPS and relative TSR, but the company paid large opioid settlements and still carries $5,058M of long-term litigation liabilities.

b6.evidence: Rather than empire-building, McKesson sold a minority of its Medical-Surgical business and plans to separate it, while keeping acquisitions focused on oncology and specialty.

roic.evidence: Returns on invested capital are very high because the business runs on negative working capital (current ratio 0.89), but equity is negative after buybacks and debt rose to $9,729M at June 30, 2026.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $5,410M against net income of $4,762M, and FCF was $3.6-5.4B in each of FY2022-FY2026.

b10.evidence: The share price rose from about $208 at the end of October 2021 to $1,004.84 in October 2026, far more than the profits the company retained, as earnings grew and the share count fell.

safety.evidence: At $1,004.84 the price is above a Nash-style DCF value of about $814 per share (12% discount rate) and above the average analyst target, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 22.5x FY2027 adjusted EPS guidance ($44.20-$45.00) and a 4.6% FCF yield are reasonable for 13-16% targeted EPS growth, but not cheap.

mu5.evidence: Demand for medicines is steady and the oligopoly is stable, but failure paths exist: loss of CVS (about 24% of revenue), drug-pricing reform, new litigation or disintermediation by manufacturers or Amazon.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in oncology and retina practices and technology services, but the core business needs little capital, so most cash goes to buybacks ($4,750M in FY2026).

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with fast-grower traits: steady drug-volume growth plus buybacks, with a simple story of 13-16% annual adjusted EPS growth.

ly3.evidence: A forward P/E of about 22.5x is above its 13-15% guided adjusted EPS growth for FY2027.

runway.evidence: Analysts expect revenue to rise from $403.4B to about $496.9B by FY2029 (about 7% a year), driven by specialty and GLP-1 drugs, but the market is mostly mature North America.

ly7.evidence: The company is shrinking its share count (diluted shares from 160.6M in FY2021 to 119.2M in Q1 FY2027), but insiders have been small net sellers, not buyers.

ly8.evidence: McKesson operates a boring niche but is well covered by Wall Street, with about 16 analysts and 85% institutional ownership.

fi2.evidence: McKesson keeps adding services such as oncology practice networks, Ontada data and CoverMyMeds technology, though these are acquisitions and services more than new products.

fi3.evidence: McKesson does not report a meaningful R&D line; its innovation is in technology services and acquisitions, whose returns are not separately disclosed.

fi4.evidence: It has won and kept the largest accounts (top ten customers about 73% of revenue), but distribution contracts are won largely on price.

longterm.evidence: Management targets steady 13-16% adjusted EPS growth and spends heavily on buybacks, while also investing in oncology and technology platforms for the long run.

gr1.evidence: McKesson had $403.4B of FY2026 revenue and a market value of about $117B.

ni10.evidence: McKesson reported a net loss of $(4,539)M in FY2021 because of opioid litigation charges.

gr4.evidence: McKesson has paid dividends since 1984 and has not cut its dividend in 26 years, and it raised the quarterly dividend to $0.94 in 2026.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS reached $38.38 in FY2026, versus $7.26 in FY2022 and a loss in FY2021, and adjusted EPS more than doubled from $17.21 in FY2021 to $39.11.

gr6.evidence: The price of $1,004.84 is about 35x the FY2024-FY2026 average GAAP EPS of $28.83.

gr7.evidence: Stockholders' equity is a deficit of $(4,240)M, so price-to-book is not meaningful and the P/E alone (about 27x trailing) is above Graham's limit.

th1.evidence: Its distribution capabilities are comparable to Cencora's and Cardinal's; it has no technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Timing is favourable for volumes as GLP-1 and specialty drugs grow (Oncology & Multispecialty revenue +31% in FY2026), but it is not a business at the start of a new technology wave.

th3.evidence: McKesson grew through more than a century of consolidation of a large existing market rather than starting with a big share of a small new one.

team.evidence: CEO Brian Tyler and the team have executed well (adjusted EPS up from $17.21 to $39.11 in five years), but this is a strong professional management team, not founder-led.

th5.evidence: McKesson's distribution network, with about 40,000 deliveries a day and contracts with CVS and GPOs, is itself the channel to customers.

durable.evidence: Drug distribution has been a stable three-player market for decades, and the scale needed to serve pharmacies nationally makes disruption over 10-20 years unlikely, though policy could reshape economics.

th7.evidence: Its oncology and data strategy is shared by Cencora and Cardinal, which also own specialty practice networks.

trend.evidence: It benefits from aging populations and the rise of specialty and GLP-1 drugs, but not from a platform shift like AI or cloud.

dr1.evidence: McKesson beat Q1 FY2027 consensus ($9.93 vs about $9.56) and raised FY2027 adjusted EPS guidance to $44.20-$45.00, implying 13-15% growth.

dr2.evidence: Completing the Wellverse (Medical-Surgical) separation and growing oncology could improve the mix in 18-24 months, but much of this is already in the stock at record highs.

dr4.evidence: The business is largely insensitive to the economy (beta about 0.3), but higher rates raise its borrowing costs and it gains little from liquidity.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include the planned Medical-Surgical (Wellverse) separation, continued buybacks and quarterly results such as the Q2 FY2027 report due in November 2026.

dr7.evidence: With a stock at record highs, thin margins and policy risk, conviction is not high enough for a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: FY2026 gross margin was only 3.6% ($14,550M on $403,430M revenue).

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $5,410M is about a 4.6% yield on a market value of about $117B, reasonable for a stable but low-growth business.

gb2.evidence: FY2026 operating income of $6,212M is about 5.1% of an enterprise value of about $122B, a modest earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback; revenue grew 12.4% in FY2026 and the stock is at a record high.

pa4.evidence: Medicines are essential and McKesson's scale is entrenched, so permanent loss is unlikely, though overpaying at the current price is a risk.

wo1.evidence: McKesson is a drug distributor, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Distribution costs fall slowly with scale; there is no rapid cost decline unlocking large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Analysts expect revenue to grow only about 7% a year, so the addressable market will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Drug demand is steady through cycles and the stock's beta is about 0.3, though drug-pricing policy and rates affect it.

ns1.evidence: Its scale lowers drug acquisition costs that it shares with large customers through competitive pricing, but rivals of similar scale do the same.

ns4.evidence: Its position should remain strong, but disintermediation and drug-pricing reform make it hard to say it will be clearly stronger in 10-20 years.

va2.evidence: It solves the large problem of getting thousands of drugs safely to tens of thousands of pharmacies and clinics every day.

tn1.evidence: McKesson is an old distribution business (founded in 1833) riding specialty and GLP-1 drug growth, not a company built for a new secular technology trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a drug wholesaler, while McKesson is shifting toward oncology practice services, data and biopharma technology, but these remain a small share of revenue.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap U.S. company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year from FY2021 to FY2026 and it earned $4,762M in FY2026, passing two of three, though debt ($9,729M) exceeds cash ($5,164M).

tn5.evidence: Debt exceeded cash at June 30, 2026 ($9,729M vs $5,164M) and Q1 FY2027 free cash flow was negative at $(372)M.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 12.4% in FY2026 and 7.7% in Q1 FY2027, and consensus expects about 7% growth in FY2027.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 12.4% plus an FCF margin of 1.3% gives about 14, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2026 revenue grew 12.4% while total GAAP operating expenses fell from $8,901M to $8,338M.

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: debt above cash, an operating margin of 1.5% (below 20%) and consensus revenue growth of about 7%.

tn10.evidence: It still carries $5,058M of long-term litigation liabilities from opioid settlements and faces drug-pricing policy risk (IRA negotiation, most-favored-nation pricing).

tn11.evidence: McKesson provides drug distribution and practice services that help pharmacies, hospitals and clinics get medicines reliably and cheaply, and charges a small markup plus service fees; customers choose it for scale and breadth.

tn13.evidence: Total about 50/130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5 (12.4%), operating margin 0, short interest 10 (about 2%), institutional ownership 10 (85%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 10, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture and mission 0, talent 0 (judged harshly).

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year, but operating margin did not expand every year (1.58% in FY2023, 1.27% in FY2024), FCF fell in FY2024 to $3,627M, and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is strong (about 25x in FY2026), but at June 30, 2026 the current ratio was 0.89, assets excluding goodwill ($77.1B) were below liabilities ($89.6B) and equity was negative.

tn18.evidence: Brian Tyler has a strong execution record and has been CEO since 2019, but he is not a founder, has under 10 years in the role and there is no record of open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: McKesson has beaten adjusted EPS consensus in recent quarters, including Q1 FY2027 ($9.93 vs about $9.56) and Q4 FY2026, though Q4 FY2026 revenue missed.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown or co-CEO, no auditor change (Deloitte) and no accounting suspicion, but gross margin has been declining with mix and insiders sold small amounts while the stock rose.

tn22.evidence: It has $403.4B of revenue, $4,762M of net income and shrinks its share count through buybacks, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At a 12% discount rate and a 1.3% FCF margin, the $1,004.84 price implies about 18-19% annual revenue growth for five years, above the 13.4% three-year average and about 7% consensus.

tn25.evidence: Using 13.4% average growth, a 1.32% average FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and net debt of $4,565M, value is about $814 per share, below $1,004.84.

tn26.evidence: At about 22.5x FY2027 adjusted EPS guidance and 13-15% EPS growth, the PEG is about 1.5-1.7, above 1.
